episodes.title: Agents That Write Their Own Tools at Runtime — Sandhya Subramani, AWS
episodes.description:
This agent starts with zero tools. Ask it for something it can't do, and it writes the tool and uses it without restarting.

Sandhya Subramani, senior developer advocate for GenAI at AWS, demos meta-tooling with the open-source Strands Agents SDK. That means agents that write, load and use their own tools at runtime, and even spin up their own sub-agents. All it takes is a system prompt describing what a good tool looks like, plus three tools: editor, shell and load_tool. She walks through agentic patterns (swarm, graph, handoff, workflow), demos a travel planner that builds its own sub-agents, and covers the evals and guardrails you need before trusting a self-modifying agent in production.

In this talk:
• Meta-tooling: editor, shell and load_tool plus one system prompt
• Agents that create their own sub-agents
• Evals for self-modifying agents: goal success, tool choice, parameters, inter-agent flow
• Guardrails: sandboxed execution, constrained permissions and observability

episodes.title: AI Coding Agents Are Breaking Big Codebases — Dan Adler, Sourcegraph
episodes.description:
Claude Code can make the change. But what if you have 90,000 repositories to make it in?

Dan Adler, CEO of Sourcegraph, makes the case for the people who own the huge, decades-old codebases that run banks, cars and airlines. Coding agents are producing a tidal wave of code, and those codebases are starting to decay through duplicated code, drifting standards, brittle dependencies and new vulnerabilities. Agents understand code by searching, but you can't grep what you can't see. Dan argues that large-scale code visibility is infrastructure, and introduces Sourcegraph's Agentic Batch Changes for making changes across thousands of repos from a single prompt.

In this talk:
• Why most software engineers work in large, long-lived codebases
• How AI-generated code accelerates codebase decay
• Why context, not model quality, is the bottleneck at enterprise scale
• Making and auditing changes across thousands of repos

episodes.title: Keyword Search Is Dying. Is Your Catalog Ready for AI Agents? — PayPal
episodes.description:
Shoppers are moving from typing keywords to describing what they need, and agents are doing the searching.

Nixon Dinh, director of product for agentic commerce at PayPal, explains how shopping is moving from the search era to the intent era and then the delegation era, and why product catalogs built for keyword SEO aren't ready for AI agents. He breaks down keyword vs semantic search and shares the results of PayPal's experiments enriching merchant product data. Enrichment consistently improved agent recommendations and thin catalogs gained the most, but over-enriching with unstructured boilerplate diluted the signal and made agents hallucinate.

In this talk:
• Search era, intent era, delegation era: how shopping behavior is shifting
• Why catalogs syndicated for ads aren't readable by agents
• Keyword vs semantic search, and why hybrid wins
• Enrichment patterns that help, and why more text isn't better

episodes.title: We Built an AI Support Agent That Resolves 80% of Tickets — AssemblyAI
episodes.description:
1,000 API signups a day and one onboarding engineer. So AssemblyAI built Joey.

Matt Lawler, forward deployed engineer lead at AssemblyAI, shares how his team replaced an off-the-shelf support bot that resolved 10% of conversations with their own agent, Joey, which resolves 80% end to end for about $700 a month. Joey is built on the Claude Agent SDK with docs checked out as local markdown, embeddings for retrieval, agentic file search and a large CLAUDE.md. It's deployed on Railway so fixes ship in about 30 seconds. Then Matt gives Joey a voice with AssemblyAI's Voice Agent API and demos it live, making the case that FDEs should automate themselves out of a job and dogfood the product their customers build.

In this talk:
• Why the FDE model doesn't scale to 1,000 signups a day
• Joey's architecture: local markdown docs, embeddings, agentic search and a single CLAUDE.md
• Turning every escalation into a roadmap item for the agent
• Adding real-time voice with one websocket: speech-to-text, LLM and text-to-speech

episodes.title: Dashboards Are Dead — Sarah Simionescu, Composio
episodes.description:
Sarah used Datadog every day for six months without ever opening the dashboard.

Sarah Simionescu, member of technical staff at Composio and on the team behind the Composio dashboard, makes the case that the dashboard is dead. She traces how we got here: five tools and five query languages, then the AI 'sparkle button', then MCP. She explains why MCP alone is still a mess (agents don't learn, too many tools drown the model, every app is isolated) and shows how an interface designed for agents fixes it. Live demos go from a Slack bug report to a fix PR, and run a cross-app analysis across PostHog and Metabase without loading full results into context.

In this talk:
• Why every dashboard and query language was a translation layer
• Three reasons wiring up a dozen MCP servers falls apart
• How tool search plus execution plans help agents work across apps
• Building products for a new kind of user: agents

episodes.title: Stop Fine-Tuning to Fix Retrieval Problems — Anant Srivastava
episodes.description:
Most AI teams never decide where their knowledge lives. Six months of normal product work decides for them.

Anant Srivastava, principal technologist for data and AI platforms at Oracle, argues that prompt, memory and weights aren't a ladder you climb when answers go wrong. They're three tools for three jobs. Through a support assistant that kept inventing product names after a fine-tune, he shows how architecture builds up by accident. He then gives a simple diagnostic for each: the prompt is for small, stable behavior; memory is for knowledge that's current, large, citable or access-controlled; weights are only for reflexes that have stopped changing. He closes with a circulating architecture where the agent gets better by doing its job.

In this talk:
• How every prompt edit, indexed doc and training sample is an architecture decision
• The diagnostic question for prompt, memory and weights
• Why you fine-tune reflexes, not facts
• Moving knowledge between context, memory and weights over time

episodes.title: What Makes Open Models Fast in Production — Sujee Maniyam, Nebius
episodes.description:
Open models have nearly caught up with proprietary ones. Serving them fast and cheaply is the hard part.

Dylan Bristot, who leads product marketing for Nebius Token Factory, and developer advocate Sujee Maniyam explain what it takes to run open LLMs in production. Dylan covers the trade-off between closed APIs and self-hosting, and the inference → data → post-training → deployment loop. Sujee then goes layer by layer through the optimizations behind fast inference: NVFP4 on the latest NVIDIA hardware, engine selection, cache-aware routing, speculative decoding with custom draft models, KV cache offloading, disaggregated prefill and decode, and finding the quantization sweet spot.

In this talk:
• Why open models are now competitive, and what that means for cost and lock-in
• Cache-aware routing versus naive load balancing for LLMs
• Speculative decoding and training draft models on your own traffic
• KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation and quantization trade-offs

episodes.title: GPU Died. Training Didn't: Self-Healing Training at Scale — Crusoe
episodes.description:
Across thousands of GPUs, hardware failures are guaranteed. Fixing them by hand at 3 a.m. doesn't scale.

Connor Guerrero, Young Jeong and Nikhil Gupta from Crusoe explain why they built Managed Slurm on top of Kubernetes. Slurm gives researchers gang scheduling, topology awareness and familiar sbatch workflows, but falls short on dynamic resources, node health and observability. Kubernetes fills those gaps without either team changing how it works. They walk through AutoClusters' fully automatic remediation of an XID 79 GPU failure, then demo killing a GPU mid-training and resuming from checkpoint in under 15 minutes with no human action.

In this talk:
• Where traditional Slurm excels for training and where it falls short
• Why one stack beats separate Slurm and Kubernetes infrastructure
• The automatic remediation flow: notify, drain, replace, requeue, resume
• Sharing GPUs between training and inference as demand shifts

episodes.title: An Interaction Is All You Need — Ivan Leo, Google DeepMind
episodes.description:
Models became agents, and the APIs didn't keep up. Google DeepMind rebuilt them.

Ivan Leo, developer experience engineer at Google DeepMind, introduces the Gemini Interactions API and Managed Agents. He traces how we went from single completions to function calling to agents, then shows server-side state with interaction IDs (no more hand-managing thought signatures), strongly typed multimodal outputs, mixing built-in and custom tools, and the new steps data model. He then demos Managed Agents, which run the Antigravity harness in a persistent remote sandbox with environment IDs, loadable sources, a credential-injecting proxy and named agents, plus the open-source Gemini API CLI.

In this talk:
• Why agent workloads need a different API shape
• Server-side state: interaction IDs and thought signatures
• Chaining image, video and audio generation with the same context
• Managed Agents: persistent sandboxes, skills, secure credentials and named agents

episodes.title: I Built a Personal AI Agent on a Raspberry Pi — Jeremy Adams, Neo4j
episodes.description:
No Mac Mini, no laptop agent. Jeremy Adams runs his personal AI agent on an old Raspberry Pi he wears around his neck.

Jeremy Adams, senior developer advocate at Neo4j, assembles a wearable AI agent live on stage: NanoClaw on a Raspberry Pi 4B, messaged over WhatsApp, with Docker-isolated agents and a Neo4j graph database. He shows how he built graph memory using the POLE schema (person, object, location, event) mid-flight, added voice-to-text through a USB mic and a hardware button, ran an offline mode with a local Neo4j, and walked the AI Engineer expo floor turning booth notes into a graph of themes. He finishes by upgrading to Neo4j Agent Memory.

In this talk:
• Why a small, hackable claw beats a feature-rich agent on your laptop
• Connecting an agent to Neo4j over MCP
• Graph memory with the POLE schema
• Offline-first capture with a local graph that syncs and enriches in the cloud
